*References:*

@[expose] public section

open scoped Nat

namespace Erdos646

/--
Let $p_1,\ldots,p_k$ be distinct primes. Are there infinitely many $n$ such that $n!$ is
divisible by an even power of each of the $p_i$?

The answer is yes, proved by Berend [Be97], who further proved that the sequence of such $n$
has bounded gaps (where the bound depends on the initial set of primes).
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/1d7b3f00780b85ed0462e79a1cd5650ee9055655/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos646.lean"]
theorem erdos_646 : answer(True) ↔
    ∀ S : Finset ℕ, (∀ p ∈ S, p.Prime) →
      {n : ℕ | ∀ p ∈ S, Even (padicValNat p (n !))}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end Erdos646

reformulations.difference: The Lean follows erdosproblems.com word for word: any finite set of distinct primes (a `Finset`), and infinitely many n with every p-adic valuation v_p(n!) even. The older sources phrase it differently. zbMATH's review of Berend (Zbl 0874.11025) quotes the Erdős–Graham [ErGr80] question as "Does there exist, for every k, some n>1 with all exponents α_1(n),…,α_k(n) even?", where p_1 < p_2 < … are the primes in order. Berend's abstract states his theorem as: for any k, infinitely many n in whose n! all of the first k primes appear to even exponents. So the older forms use the first k primes rather than an arbitrary finite set, and ErGr80 asks for some n>1 rather than infinitely many n. A reader comparing with ErGr80 p.77 or Be97 might think the Lean states something stronger.
reformulations.equivalence_argument:
All three universal statements are equivalent.
(1) The Lean form implies the first-k-primes forms: take S = {first k primes}; an infinite set contains some n > 1.
(2) First k primes with infinitely many n implies the Lean form: any finite set of primes lies inside the first K primes for some K, and the evenness condition for the larger set implies it for the subset.
(3) First k primes with some n>1 implies the Lean form. Fix S and N, and pick K > N + max S. Take n > 1 with v_{p_i}(n!) even for all i < K. By Bertrand's postulate there is a prime q with n/2 < q ≤ n, and then v_q(n!) = 1, which is odd. So q is not among the first K primes, which forces n ≥ q > N. Hence the set for S has elements above every N and is infinite.
I proved both `↔`s in Lean against this repo's Mathlib (`fc_iff_firstk_exists` and `fc_iff_firstk_infinite`, using `Nat.exists_prime_lt_and_le_two_mul` and `padicValNat_factorial`), with axioms [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound] only.

review.notes:
No findings.

1. Reading of the source. \"n! is divisible by an even power of each p_i\" means the exact exponent v_{p_i}(n!) is even. Berend's title and abstract confirm this (\"all first k primes appear to even exponents\"). The file uses `Even (padicValNat p (n !))`; printing with notation off shows the body is `padicValNat p n.factorial`. Requiring the exponent to be positive would change nothing, because v_p(n!) ≥ 1 once n ≥ max S.

2. Boundary cases. `S = ∅` (k = 0) is trivially true for that single S and does not make the universal statement trivial. `n = 0` has `0! = 1` and valuation 0, which does not affect infinitude. `#eval` on small cases looked right; e.g. S = {2, 3} gives 0, 1, 6, 7, 10, 11, …

3. `formal_proof` check. The linked theorem is `infinitely_many_even_factorial_exponents (k) (p : Fin k → ℕ) (hp : ∀ i, (p i).Prime) (h_distinct : Function.Injective p) : Set.Infinite {n | ∀ i, partial_sum k p n i = 0}`, where `partial_sum` is `padicValNat (p i) n!` cast to `ZMod 2`. I proved in Lean that this implies the file's statement. The linked file targets v4.29.1 and fails verbatim on this repo's v4.33.1 in three places:
   - line 105: \"no goals\";
   - line 384: `decide` on a `ZMod 2` goal;
   - line 678: an extra instance goal from `convert`.
   These are toolchain-drift errors. After patching only those three proof lines (no statement changes), the whole file compiles here with axioms [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]. Inside that file I derived the exact `True ↔ ∀ S …` statement with the same clean axioms.

4. Status and references. `research solved` with `answer(True)` matches erdosproblems.com (\"PROVED (LEAN)\", solved in the affirmative) and the teorth database. The module docstring's references (ErGr80, Er97e, Be97) match the site's citation header \"[ErGr80,p.77] [Er97e]\" plus Be97.

5. Not formalized, and not a defect. Berend's bounded-gaps strengthening appears only as a docstring remark, not as a variant.

6. Sources I could not read directly. I had no text of ErGr80 p.77 or Er97e, and only Berend's abstract rather than the full paper. The ErGr80 wording used in the reformulation entry is the one quoted in zbMATH's review, and I proved it equivalent to the Lean statement. The faithfulness verdict relies on erdosproblems.com, the cited statement, and does not depend on these texts.
